articles.title: Destroyed in Operation Sindoor, JeM's Bahawalpur terror base fully operational again
articles.summary: Pakistan News: NEW DELHI: Extensive restoration work has concluded at the Markaz Subhanallah facility, the primary base for the UN-sanctioned terrorist group Jaish-e.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Extensive restoration work has concluded at the Markaz Subhanallah facility, the primary base for the UN-sanctioned terrorist group Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM), a little over a year after the compound suffered severe structural destruction during India's Operation Sindoor retaliatory strikes.Fresh footage indicates it is fully operational again, complete with reconstructed domes, updated interior plastering, new paint, and premium marble flooring that conceals previous blast damage.Deep blast zones within the primary hall were filled with concrete, while ruined satellite buildingsâincluding the Al-Sabir seminary and housing units for leadershipâwere demolished to enable new construction.Intelligence reports indicate that Pakistani authorities channeled 250 million PKR in cash to JeM, with approximately 110 million PKR dedicated specifically to restoring the central complex over a 15-month period.With JeM leader Masood Azhar incapacitated by health issues, day-to-day command of the Bahawalpur facility has shifted to his brothers, Talha Al-Saif and Mohinuddin Aurangzeb (also known as Ammar Alvi).Meanwhile, senior figures Masood Azhar and Rauf Asghar remain harbored under government protection in the Nawabshah district of Sindh, sources said.ALSO READ | Operation Sindoor exposed limits of Pakistan's nuclear deterrenceCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia likely to mobilize at least 300,000 more troops to Ukraine war, Zelensky warns
articles.summary: Russia is likely to mobilize another 300,000 troops later this year, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as it tries to complete the capture of a long-coveted region of east Ukraine.
articles.body: Russia is likely to mobilize another 300,000 troops later this year, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as it tries to complete the capture of a long-coveted region of east Ukraine. In wide-ranging remarks released Sunday, Zelensky said he expected that the Russians would end the year occupying the same amount of Ukrainian territory as at the beginning of the year, despite enormous losses of manpower. “Russia has lost 267,000 personnel since the start of the year, including around 155,000 killed to date,” Zelensky claimed. The figure is impossible to confirm but in line with estimates by Western officials. Russian parliamentary elections take place next month, and there has been speculation about a fresh mobilization despite a 2022 draft triggering protests and an exodus of young men. “We are confident that following the elections, they will carry out a mobilization. We believe this will not take place in the major cities,” Zelensky said. Zelensky said he believed Putin would “deploy the 300,000 newly mobilized troops depending on the situation in the east of our country,” and had told his generals to complete the occupation of Donetsk by the end of the year. “They’ll lose all 300,000 of these newly mobilized Russians there; we’ll wipe them out,” Zelensky asserted. Ukrainian units are defending some 20% of Donetsk, including a belt of strategic industrial towns such as Slaviansk and Kramatorsk. Zelensky said it was impossible for the Russians to complete the capture of Donetsk region. He suggested the Russians might also attempt an incursion into the northern Ukrainian regions of Kharkiv and Sumy. “They do not yet have troops in the Bryansk region (which borders northern Ukraine), but we can see military equipment along the borders with the Russian Federation.” Musk, Kushner, and air defenses On air defenses, Zelensky contrasted the number of Patriot missiles supplied in 2023 – which was 675 – with the forecast number of 264 this year. Ballistic missile attacks have increased civilian casualties and infrastructure damage across Ukraine - and Patriots are the only means of shooting them down. “As you can see, there is, unfortunately, a downward trend, and this depends primarily on the American side,” he said. Last month, US President Donald Trump suggested Ukraine would be permitted to build Patriot missiles on license, but later backed away from the idea. If the US would supply up to 10% of its Patriot missile stocks to Ukraine, Kyiv would pay for them, Zelensky said. Such a commitment “could make a huge difference, both in terms of saving lives and diplomatically as well.” Ukraine faces the same problem in acquiring Aster air defense missiles from Europe, according to Zelensky, despite a recent pledge by French president Emmanuel Macron. “There aren’t enough ‘Aster’ missiles, even though they are being produced,” he said – though added a licensing agreement would accelerate supplies. Kyiv’s long-range missile program will get a boost Monday when new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham makes his first official visit to Ukraine. London has agreed to allow defense firm MBDA to release classified information on UK components to help Ukraine build its own long-range SCALP missiles, the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow. In the meantime, Ukraine is hunting the sites in Russia from where ballistic missiles are launched, according to Zelensky. Russia’s military industries may be capable of building about 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, Zelensky said. “There are specific objectives regarding strikes on military targets and other anti-ballistic sanctions,” he said. Ukraine has developed an arsenal of long-range drones and its own cruise missiles which are being used against a widening array of targets inside Russia. He also spoke about Kyiv’s efforts to get permission to use Starlink satellite imagery of Russian territory. Elon Musk, who owns Starlink, said he “believed that this could lead to a major escalation against the Russian Federation on Ukraine’s part,” according to Zelensky. “He said he was in favor of ending the war, not prolonging it” – and discussions with Washington were continuing. As for negotiations, Zelensky suggested that the window of opportunity for ending the war stretched through the end of next summer, when the US presidential election campaign would begin. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were “finding it very difficult to find a format whereby the Russians would agree to end this war without Ukraine having to withdraw from Donbas or accept other unacceptable solutions.” “Jared, Steve and I agreed to summarize all these discussions on a single page – setting out the realistic options for ending the war. This is what the Americans want to discuss with us and with the Russians.”

articles.title: Pasta factory expansion leads to stunning discovery of 2,600-year-old city of the dead
articles.summary: Pasta Garofalo's factory expansion in Gragnano uncovered burial chambers with grave goods connecting Greek, Egyptian and Etruscan civilizations.
articles.body: A pasta factory expansion in Italy took an unexpected turn when archaeologists uncovered a 2,600-year-old city of the dead, filled with ancient tombs and rare treasures. The necropolis was found at the Pasta Garofalo factory in Gragnano, a town near Naples, according to a news release issued by the company. The excavation was conducted between 2025 and 2026 ahead of an expansion of Pasta Garofalo's production facility, with the findings recently announced by the company in July. 2,000-YEAR-OLD ROMAN RECIPES BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE — HERE'S WHAT THEY ACTUALLY TASTE LIKE The site, which dates to the first half of the sixth century B.C., was built during the Archaic period of Mediterranean history, centuries before the rise of the Roman Empire. Pictures from the excavation show rows of stone burial chambers at the site, along with human remains, pottery and other artifacts. Several burial chambers contained rarely preserved materials, including textiles, wooden objects and woven baskets, which officials said "deepen[s] understanding of funerary practices, social organization and everyday life during the Archaic period." Officials also reported that the grave goods found at the site were "remarkable" and included Egyptian scarabs, animal-shaped amber ornaments and "silver and bronze artifacts of Etruscan origin." ARCHAEOLOGISTS REVEAL NUTRITIOUS FOOD REMAINS DISCOVERED IN ANCIENT VILLA QUARTERS "These exceptional finds testify to the central role played by the ancient territory of Gragnano within Mediterranean trade networks, serving as a crossroads connecting the Greek, Egyptian and Etruscan worlds," the statement read. The discovery held special significance for Pasta Garofalo, the company said, given its centuries-old ties to Gragnano and its pasta-making tradition. Pasta Garofalo "has celebrated the deep bond between pasta and the town of Gragnano ... [and] this relationship has been further enriched by an extraordinary new chapter," according to the release. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Massimo Menna, chief executive officer of Pasta Garofalo, said the discovery "fills us with great pride and a profound sense of responsibility." "Our history is inseparably linked to Gragnano, a place that has safeguarded a unique heritage of culture, tradition and manufacturing expertise for centuries," Menna said. "We believe that doing business also means caring for the places where we operate, contributing to their knowledge and enhancement." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Researchers will continue studying the human remains to learn more about the ancient community's diet, movements and living conditions. "Ongoing research will prioritize the analysis of the osteological remains to examine diets, mobility patterns and living conditions of the communities that occupied the region during the Archaic period," the statement noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The discovery follows other significant necropolis-related finds across Italy in recent years. Earlier this year, officials found the remains of an ancient sanctuary in northern Italy after construction crews unexpectedly uncovered the site while working on a new highway. articles.title: Pakistan army chief Asim Munir to visit Iran amid push to revive stalled US talks
articles.summary: Middle East News: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will travel to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders as Islamabad seeks to revive stalled effor.
articles.body: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will travel to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders as Islamabad seeks to revive stalled efforts to bring the United States and Iran back to the negotiating table.Iran's foreign ministry announced the visit on Sunday, saying Munir will discuss bilateral ties and regional issues during his stay. He will be accompanied by a delegation that is expected to hold high-level discussions with the Iranian leadership.The visit comes as Pakistan steps up efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran after an agreement intended to create a 60-day window for high-level peace talks fell apart last month.Pakistan's mediation effortsPakistan had signed the interim peace agreement as a guarantor. However, the arrangement broke down as tensions in West Asia intensified and the US and Iran resumed military strikes.Pakistan has since been trying to restart the diplomatic process. Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi travelled to Tehran earlier this month, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that Munir's visit would focus on strengthening cooperation between the two countries and supporting efforts to promote peace and security in the region.Pakistan has not yet officially commented on the army chief's planned visit.Why the talks broke downThe stalled process followed a memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June. The agreement was intended to provide a 60-day period for high-level negotiations aimed at restoring peace in West Asia.However, the talks collapsed after tensions between Washington and Tehran escalated again in mid-July. Pakistan's subsequent attempts to bring the two sides back to negotiations have so far failed to produce a breakthrough.A major obstacle is the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route that has been disrupted by the conflict. The war began on February 28 after the US and Israel launched joint attacks on Iran, prompting retaliatory strikes from Tehran. Under normal circumstances, around one-fifth of the world's energy supplies passes through the Gulf chokepoint.Iran warns against economic pressureIranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended the June agreement as the best way for Tehran to move beyond what he described as a situation of âneither war nor peaceâ.At the same time, Mohsen Rezaei, the hard-line new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned neighbouring countries against joining a fresh US effort to put pressure on Iran's economy.US President Donald Trump had warned on August 20 that Washington would launch what he called the âmost crushing economic operationâ against Iran if Tehran failed to reach a deal.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump accuses Canada of wanting ‘benefits of being a State, without being one’ amid trade war
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday claimed that Canada desires the “benefits of being a state, without being one” amid trade tensions between the U.S. and its northern neighbor. “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” the…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday claimed that Canada desires the “benefits of being a state, without being one” amid trade tensions between the U.S. and its northern neighbor.

“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” the president said in an early Sunday morning Truth Social post.

On Saturday , Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that his country would implement retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. starting on Sept. 8, responding to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent tariffs which just went into effect.

During a press conference, Carney said that Canada would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

The prime minister said Ottawa would offer additional details about the retaliatory tariffs in the “coming days,” with the tariffs applying to goods including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

Carney emphasized during the press conference that his government takes “this step reluctantly.”

Trump has previously discussed adding Canada as the U.S.’s 51st state, but Canadian leaders have repeatedly pushed back on the idea. During the president’s second term, he has also gotten into tariff fights with Ottawa, souring relations with a reliable American ally.

Earlier this year, Trump quipped about Carney being the “future Governor of Canada,” bringing back an insult previously used against the prime minister’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

“I’m working with Governor Gretchen Whitmer [D-Mich.] on trying to save The Great Lakes from the rather violent and destructive Asian Carp, which is rapidly taking over Lake Michigan, and all of the beautiful surrounds,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the time.

“I’ll be asking other Governors to join into this fight, including those of Illinois, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, New York and, of course, the future Governor of Canada, Mark Carney, who I know will be happy to contribute to this worthy cause,” he added.

articles.title: Moke brushes Hawaii’s Big Island just a week after Hurricane Lala
articles.summary: Tropical Depression Moke is passing well south of Hawaii after weakening Sunday evening, but flooding rainfall is still possible on Monday.
articles.body: Tropical Depression Moke is passing well south of Hawaii after weakening Sunday evening, but flooding rainfall is still possible on Monday. Moke is the state’s second tropical threat in a week following Hurricane Lala’s deadly blow to the islands. But Moke has been far less impactful than Lala because it’s much weaker and has tracked much farther south. 🌧️ Get your local forecast in the CNN Weather app Rainfall is the system’s biggest threat — and it’s falling on some of the same places that Lala flooded. This means it takes far less rainfall to trigger “life-threatening flooding and mudslides,” the National Hurricane Center warned. Parts of the Big Island had picked up over 1 inch of rain through late Sunday night, local time. Moke could still spin some additional downpours into the Big Island on Monday, especially in windward and southeast parts of the island. A flood watch remains in effect through the afternoon. The islands’ steep slopes force air upward, where it cools and releases its moisture as rain. An additional 3 to 6 inches of rain could fall in limited parts of the Big Island through Monday. Eastern Maui is also forecast to receive 3 to 6 inches, while western Maui and the remainder of the islands could see up to 1 or 2 inches. Moke is forecast to continue weakening as it moves westward away from Hawaii early this week. The depression is forecast to dissipate on Tuesday, but it could fall apart even sooner. Hawaii Volcanoes National Park closed on Friday until further notice in advance of the storm. The park still doesn’t have power, internet or phone lines after Lala swept by last week, and many of its employees are still recovering from the storm. Lala’s eyewall brushed the southern coast of the Big Island while its center was roughly 30 miles offshore. Moke’s center passed over 300 miles south and southwest of the Big Island on Sunday and Sunday night during its closest approach.

Police cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to trace the attackers.No individual or group has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.Five policemen injured in grenade attackIn a separate incident in Mohmand district, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil, police said.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, cross-border movement of fighters and military operations.Pakistan's federal government has blamed the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) for attacks in areas bordering Afghanistan since a ceasefire agreement between the two sides ended in November 2022.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Europe News: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that holding elections during the ongoing war with Russia could fracture the country and even âdest.
articles.body: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that holding elections during the ongoing war with Russia could fracture the country and even âdestroyâ it, as fresh calls grow for Kyiv to hold a vote despite martial law.Ukraine has suspended elections under martial law since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, with the move continuing to receive broad public support as the country remains focused on the war.Zelenskyy was responding to a call by ousted former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov for Ukraine to find a way to organise fresh elections despite the ongoing conflict. Fedorov's demand has emerged as a direct challenge to Zelenskyy's leadership.âI believe that if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections during this kind of war,â Zelenskyy said at a briefing with selected journalists, according to Reuters.He later warned that an election held under current conditions could further fracture the country.âI believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,â Zelenskyy said.The issue has nevertheless gained fresh prominence after Fedorov's call for a wartime vote. Zelenskyy has previously faced similar demands from Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump.The debate comes amid a political crisis in Kyiv that intensified after Zelenskyy dismissed Fedorov, who had remained a popular figure. The dispute was followed by criticism of Ukraine's military leadership and further changes within the top command structure.Zelenskyy's five-year presidential term formally expired in May 2024, but elections have not been held because of the continuing war.Zelenskyy said he would support an election if Ukraine's allies could establish âspecific conditionsâ to ensure it was safe, legitimate and democratic. According to an opinion poll cited by AFP, only 15 percent of Ukrainians believe elections should be held before the end of hostilities.It would require the participation of Ukrainian soldiers, people living in frontline areas and millions of Ukrainians who have fled abroad, he said. Voting would also have to take place safely, âwithout strikes and shellingâ.âThat's why my strategy is to steer the country toward an ending of the war and to preserve an independent and sovereign state,â Zelenskyy said.The debate comes as Ukraine prepares for another difficult winter. Zelenskyy said Russia had a stockpile of between 600 and 630 high-speed ballistic missiles and was seeking to produce more than 100 a month.âI wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our Air Force is 360,â he said according to the Guardian, while acknowledging constraints on global production of the interceptors.Earlier, Zelenskyy had said France had agreed to provide at least one SAMP/T air-defence system, while Germany would supply about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors in 2027-28. French President Emmanuel Macron separately said he had agreed to strengthen support for Ukraine, including interceptor missiles.The Ukrainian president also said he believed Russia could seek to mobilise another 300,000 soldiers after parliamentary elections in September, according to the Guardian.Meanwhile, a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 57 per cent of Ukrainians wanted elections only after the fighting ends, underlining the challenges facing any move towards a wartime vote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dozens of attacks in southern Thailand wound three people
articles.summary: Many local government offices and several vehicles were damaged or destroyed in the 51 attacks late on Saturday.
articles.body:
Dozens of coordinated arson and incendiary attacks across Thailand’s south left at least three people wounded and government property burned, the military has said.

Multiple local government offices and several vehicles were damaged or destroyed in the 51 attacks late on Saturday, according to the military’s Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC).

“Multiple coordinated incidents aimed at creating unrest occurred in various locations across the southern border provinces” from about 8pm (13:00 GMT) to midnight on Saturday, the ISOC said in a statement.

Firefighters worked to extinguish burning tyres left in the middle of a road and flames inside a 7-Eleven convenience store on Saturday night, while police officers stopped motorists for security checks, footage from the local broadcaster Thai PBS showed.

Most of the attacks were in Narathiwat province, where three civilians were wounded and an overnight curfew was imposed, while other attacks occurred in neighbouring Yala and Pattani provinces, authorities said.

Since 2004, a low-level conflict has simmered in the southernmost provinces of Buddhist-majority Thailand, killing more than 7,000 people, as rebels in the Muslim-majority region battle for greater autonomy.

No group has claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attacks.

Two women, aged 45 and 46, and a 21-year-old man were hurt in a roadside bombing in Narathiwat, provincial officials said in a statement.

All three were admitted to hospital and were in stable condition.

The national railway operator temporarily suspended part of a route in Narathiwat after officials found damage on the tracks “caused by a disruptive bombing incident last night”, the ISOC said.

Narathiwat Governor Boonchuay Homyamyen told local media that concerned agencies were investigating sites of the attacks on Sunday, including a local government office, telecommunications towers and electrical poles.

The Narathiwat military command earlier announced a curfew from Saturday night until 6am on Sunday.

A vehicle was stolen from the office of a subdistrict administrative organisation in Narathiwat during one of the attacks that left the building in flames, the ISOC said.

The burned-out pick-up truck was later found abandoned on a road.

At a municipal office in Pattani province, damaged in another attack, army commander for the southern region Norathip Poinok said on Sunday that the assailants had aimed to destroy the building and undermine public trust in the state.

“We had intelligence reports for about two months that there would be attacks on local offices,” he told reporters, adding that the military had issued warnings to security agencies but did not know when and where the assaults would occur.

Rebels in the far south regularly carry out attacks on security officials and government property, including before visits by officials to the region.

Last month, assailants killed five soldiers in a shooting and bomb attack at a checkpoint in Narathiwat.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and members of his cabinet are scheduled to make a two-day visit to the city of Hat Yai in southern Songkhla province next week to discuss investment projects, flood prevention and security issues, his office said on Saturday.

Formal talks between the Thai government and the National Revolutionary Front, abbreviated as BRN in the local language, the main separatist group in the south, were expected to resume in June after a rise in violence. The negotiations have struggled to resolve disagreements over self-government, security measures and political representation.

Earlier this week, Thanut Suvarnananda, head of Thailand’s National Intelligence Agency who was appointed by the government in April to lead the peace process, said he wants to move away from a transactional approach.

Thanut said he seeks to turn the BRN from an adversary into a potential partner in addressing demands from communities across Thailand’s deep south, including the predominantly Malay-Muslim provinces of Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat that were once part of the independent Malay sultanate of Patani.

articles.title: Iran warns Middle East neighbors against joining US ‘economic war’
articles.summary: Iran has advised its neighbors in the Middle East against entering an “economic war” alongside the U.S., as the conflict between Washington and Tehran nears the six-month mark. Mohsen Rezaei, the Iranian Supreme National Security Council leader, gave a heads-up to surrounding countries to not participate in an American effort to strain the Iranian economy,…
articles.body:
Iran has advised its neighbors in the Middle East against entering an “ economic war ” alongside the U.S., as the conflict between Washington and Tehran nears the six-month mark.

Mohsen Rezaei, the Iranian Supreme National Security Council leader, gave a heads-up to surrounding countries to not participate in an American effort to strain the Iranian economy, according to The Associated Press .

If President Trump “wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Rezaei told state media Saturday, per the AP.

Rezaei also said Tehran would aim for shipping routes for oil leaving the Persian Gulf if nearby countries got involved in the economic pressure against his country, the AP reported.

Last week, Trump announced the “ MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER ” targeting Iran amid talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which has been essentially closed since March. Iran and Oman have joint jurisdiction over the critical waterway, but Trump has threatened to make the strait a U.S. territory.

“This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

The president said any country that gave “any type of lifeline to Iran” would face “TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences” from the U.S.

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are,” the president wrote.

“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat,” Trump continued.

Rezaei’s comments come after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday the U.S.-Iran war should end because the world has accepted Tehran’s victory in this conflict.

articles.title: Despite contactless payments, euro banknotes in circulation have risen from about â¬1 trillion in 2016 to â¬1.6 trillion as Europeans keep emergency cash ready for crises and cyber outages
articles.summary: Europe News: Despite the widespread use of contactless payments and smartphones across Europe, people are keeping more physical cash. The value of euro banknotes i.
articles.body: Despite the widespread use of contactless payments and smartphones across Europe, people are keeping more physical cash. The value of euro banknotes in circulation has increased sharply in recent years, as fears over war, cyber-attacks and other emergencies grow.According to European Central Bank (ECB) data, as reported by The Guardian, the total value of euro banknotes in circulation increased from about â¬1 trillion in 2016 to â¬1.6 trillion in June 2026. The number of notes has also increased, with more than 31 billion banknotes now in circulation.The increase comes at a time when cash is used less often for everyday purchases in many European cities. Contactless cards, mobile phones and other digital payment methods have become common. However, people are now keeping cash because they are worried about situations in which digital payment systems may not work.Those concerns include wars, wildfires, floods, storms and cyber-attacks. In such situations, people may not be able to depend on online banking, mobile apps or contactless payment systems. Cash, therefore, can provide a way to pay for basic items when digital systems are unavailable.Why Europeans are keeping cashThe ECB's chief economist, Philip Lane, pointed to the difference between how often cash is used for transactions and how much cash people are holding.âThe total stock of banknotes is continuing to grow. In transactions, the number of notes is coming down, but in terms of the stock, it is increasing,â Lane said, as quoted by The Guradian.This means that even though people may be using fewer banknotes when buying things, the overall amount of physical money being held is rising.The increase has been linked to growing concerns about emergencies. In 2025, people in the European Union were advised to keep enough food, water and other essentials at home to last for 72 hours in case of an emergency.The advice covered possible situations such as wildfires, floods and storms, as well as cyber-attacks and other hostile events. A suggested crisis pack included bottled water, a transistor radio, canned food and cash.A major cyber-attack in the UK last year showed how such disruption can affect businesses.More notes, fewer transactionsECB data has tracked euro banknotes in circulation since 2002. The value of those banknotes has risen from around â¬1 trillion in 2016 to â¬1.6 trillion in June 2026. More than 31 billion banknotes are currently in circulation, compared with 24 billion before the pandemic in 2019.Some European countries have already given people specific advice on how much emergency cash they should keep at home. Austria, Finland, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands have recommended keeping between â¬70 and â¬100 per household.The suggested amount is intended to cover essential spending for about 72 hours if online and mobile payment services stop working.Cash matters beyond emergenciesOlive McCarthy, a professor at University College Cork who has an interest in financial inclusion, told The Guardian, keeping cash only for emergencies could create another problem.âWhile advice to maintain cash for emergencies is well made, and serves to remind us all to be prepared when digital systems let us down, it is essential that cash does not become viewed merely as a backup measure. If we stop using it when there isnât a crisis, it might not be easy to use it when there is.âMcCarthy also said cash can be important for people who may find digital payments difficult to access. She pointed to elderly and vulnerable people, as well as victims of domestic abuse who may depend on cash if their partner controls their spending. Cash can also help children learn about money, financial literacy and budgeting, she said.The ECB has also pointed to the need to maintain access to cash. Lane referred to the importance of legislation that would ensure cash machines remain available across European high streets.Keeping notes relevantECB is also working on new euro banknotes and prepares for the possible introduction of the digital euro. articles.summary: A humanoid robot named Lightning Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, edging Usain Bolt's record.
articles.body: The world's fastest man record was shattered on the first day of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. Jamaican Usain Bolt's 100-meter dash record of 9.58 set in 2009 was edged by a Beijing-based X-Humanoid robot named Lightning Bolt, which ran 100 meters at 9:39 seconds before smashing into a blue wall. Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second. After smashing into the wall, the robots were placed on a stretcher, unlike Bolt, who was able to jog a lap to celebrate human achievement in 2009. ROBOTS BEAT HUMANS IN HALF MARATHON The World Humanoid Robot Games, in its second year, features more than 2,000 robots in 51 events and 1,000 competitions like running, table tennis and soccer. The five-day event highlights China's rapid progress in robotics amid a heated tech race with the U.S. The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week Beijing was holding the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities. Humanoid robots are "evolving rapidly," said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES "At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans," she said. "But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look." "These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing," said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator. NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said that he was hoping to see "the best robots China currently has to offer." This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war. The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from China, which makes the majority of the world's humanoid robots. "I welcome these Executive Branch national security determinations, and I am pleased that the FCC has now added foreign produced advanced robotics and power inverters to the FCC’s Covered List," FCC Chair Brendan Carr wrote in a statement last month. "Following President Trump’s leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America’s critical supply chains and, with today’s action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that." articles.title: PM Tarique Rahman’s trip stalled: What it means for Bangladesh-India ties
articles.summary: India and Bangladesh have not been able to move past the contentious question of Sheikh Hasina, living in New Delhi.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first trip to India has been put on hold, highlighting the strained ties between the two South Asian neighbours since the July 2024 student-led uprising that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee the country.

Since coming to power in February, Rahman – the son of Hasina’s archrival, the late Khaleda Zia – has aimed to improve ties with India. But a press conference conducted by Hasina, who lives in India in exile, has riled Bangladesh.

Dhaka says that the August 5 press conference has “vitiated” the atmosphere, adding that “a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit” of Prime Minister Rahman.

For now, Rahman’s trip looks uncertain, as Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry said officials from both countries have been engaged in talks for “several weeks” to work out a possible solution.

Here is everything you need to know about the latest diplomatic turbulence between the South Asian neighbours.

New Delhi had extended an invitation to Rahman for a stand-alone visit to India this month, ahead of next month’s scheduled BRICS summit. BRICS is a grouping of major emerging economies, currently chaired by India.

Since Rahman took office, there have been several exchanges between top ministers and diplomats from both sides. India appointed Dinesh Trivedi, a former minister and member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as its envoy to Dhaka in a rare political appointment to the key post.

Last Tuesday, Trivedi appealed to Rahman’s government, arguing that the Indian mission is not asking Dhaka “to forget the past”, in an apparent reference to Hasina’s exile in India. “Keep the past and sort out the differences of the past. But move on. Don’t get stagnant,” he added.

At a reception hosted by the Indian High Commission in Dhaka, Trivedi said that Modi wanted Rahman’s visit to be “memorable”.

But those plans for a visit were already derailed after Dhaka took offence to Hasina virtually addressing a presser at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club in New Delhi on August 5, marking two years of her ouster.

India clarified that it had nothing to do with the event, but to no avail.

Both capitals have been tight-lipped about Rahman’s visit. “I have nothing to say right now,” said India’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, responding to a question about Rahman’s visit.

Speaking at an event on Saturday, India’s Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said India and Bangladesh’s bilateral ties must meet the “test of mutual interest”.

“It has to work for them, it has to work for us,” he said.

“There has to be a reasonable degree of my recognising and respecting what is their interest, just as I expect them also to do so,” Jaishankar said.

Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser, Humayun Kabir, told a Bangladeshi news agency that there is “no rush” in Dhaka to facilitate the prime minister’s visit to India.

Kabir added that Dhaka is still ascertaining what kind of relationship India wants with the newly elected government in Bangladesh.

“The neighbouring country must properly understand the reality of Bangladesh’s July Mass Uprising, which took place through the sacrifices of more than 1,500 people,” he said, referring to India sitting on the request for Hasina’s extradition.

Earlier this month, New Delhi had said that it was considering Hasina’s extradition request based on the established procedure. Both countries have an extradition treaty, but with an exception for political cases.

Bangladesh has made Hasina’s extradition a major issue. Hasina’s government was seen as especially close to India, and New Delhi’s backing of her authoritarian rule also angered Bangladeshis.

Dhaka has been seeking the extradition of Hasina, who was handed a death sentence in absentia in November 2025. Some analysts have accused New Delhi of using it as a diplomatic bargaining chip.

Bangladesh has expressed its displeasure with India for hosting Hasina and sees Hasina’s political speeches as an interference in its internal affairs. During the August 5 presser, Hasina said she would return to Bangladesh.

“We have requested Indian authorities to expeditiously act on our request to extradite Sheikh Hasina and other fugitive criminals,” the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry said in an X post on August 16.

“We reiterate that we will continue to pursue our ‘Bangladesh First’ policy to promote friendly bilateral relations with other countries, including our neighbours, on the basis of sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs and mutual benefit.”

For New Delhi, Dhaka inching closer to Pakistan after decades of strained ties is a major diplomatic setback. India played a major role in the formation of Bangladesh from Pakistan in 1971.

Shakil Ahmed, an assistant professor of government and politics at Dhaka’s Jahangirnagar University, noted that domestic politics tends to influence foreign policy at times.

“Relations between India and Bangladesh are constrained by their domestic politics, especially in Dhaka,” he said.

“People in Bangladesh want that any relation with India should be based on self-respect and mutual interests,” he said, adding that Rahman’s government has been diversifying its friendships with foreign countries, including the US, China, and Pakistan.

“New Delhi saw Bangladesh as one of India’s foreign policy followers,” Ahmed said, noting that that is not the case anymore. “Hasina gave India a blank cheque in foreign relations, which is not happening anymore.”

India’s Hindu nationalist government’s push to fence the 4,096km-long (2,545-mile) border with Bangladesh has also strained ties. Anti-Bangladesh rhetoric by ruling party officials has further antagonised Dhaka.

India has been deporting what it calls undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants across its borders. Dhaka has accused New Delhi of pushing people extrajudicially into Bangladesh without diplomatic verification.

Sanjay Bhardwaj, a professor of South Asian studies at the Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Rahman is playing to the gallery by stalling his maiden India visit.

Hasina’s case is one of political persecution, said Bhardwaj, pointing out that the previous government led by Hasina also targeted the opposition. Rahman lived in exile for more than 17 years in London, the United Kingdom, including all of Hasina’s years in power, after he was slapped with several criminal cases. He was convicted in absentia on money laundering charges and in a case linked to an alleged plot to assassinate Hasina.

“India has been positive to cultivate and have a developmental partnership with Bangladesh, with no reluctance to develop the economic participation,” he added. “But Rahman is interested in politics and not thinking about the development of Bangladesh.”

Hasina’s extradition is a contentious issue, he said, adding that both capitals must move beyond this to maintain a productive bilateral relationship.

Sreeradha Datta, a professor specialising in South Asian studies at India’s OP Jindal Global University, said that both countries need to talk, since “there is no alternative”.

As neighbours, “they do not have a choice to disengage”, she said, adding that merely the passage of time will not repair the relations.

“How can one have any control when there is no dialogue and engagement?” Datta asked.

“The initial warmth diluted in nationalistic noise on both sides,” Datta said, referring to initial interactions, including an Indian delegation led by Jaishankar visiting Dhaka last year for the funeral of Rahman’s mother, Khaleda Zia.

Datta argued that New Delhi needs to come to terms with a new reality that the government of Bangladesh may not share the same warmth as the one under Hasina did.

“But that doesn’t matter,” she said. “These are neighbours, and a relationship based on objectives or interests is what will take it forward.”

articles.title: Robots can outrun humans, but can they plug in a cable?
articles.summary: China’s humanoid robots have ​shown they can run quicker than the fastest humans.
articles.body: China’s humanoid robots have ​shown they can run quicker than the fastest humans. Now comes the real test: Can they also handle packaging ‌and warehouse operations while reliably performing precision tasks like connecting cables designed to evaluate their ability to work like humans in less flashy jobs? The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games, which began Saturday in Beijing, combine events modeled on human sports with those designed to test the robots in simulated factories, restaurants and ​offices and in emergency situations. The games, heavily promoted in Chinese state media, feature 51 events, including 30 sports competitions and ​21 scenario-based contests. More than 40% require robots to operate fully autonomously, according to Huawei, a tech ⁠partner of the games. On Saturday, two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt’s 9.58-second world record in the 100-meter sprint. That was a ​sharp improvement from 2025, when the winning robot’s time was more than 20 seconds. Braking was an issue, as the machines slammed into ​a thick mat that organizers placed several feet after the finish line. Another humanoid, the same model as the 100-meter champion, ran 400 meters in 39.7 seconds, faster than South African Wayde van Niekerk’s world record of 43.03 seconds. “The intensity is higher than last year, which places significant demands on the robot’s ​battery management and thermal dissipation capabilities,” said spectator and robotics investor Xu Qiaosheng. “It holds huge significance for the development of China’s industrial ​sector.” Robots will compete in tug-of-war and weightlifting, while tai chi and pitch-pot — in which contestants throw arrow-like sticks into a narrow-necked vase — will give traditional ‌Chinese ⁠sports a futuristic twist. Beyond the spectacle, the more revealing tests could come when robots encounter the small imperfections of the physical world: a cable at the wrong angle, an object just out of reach, a shifting package or a missed step. That tests whether robots can identify objects, accurately position their hands and bodies, apply controlled force and recover from errors without human intervention. Lumos Robotics ​Chief Executive Yu Chao said ​the games could help improve ⁠hardware and provide a showcase for the industry. But Yu said the longer-term value will depend on real-world problem solving. “Only when it can work in those end scenarios does it have real value,” Yu ​said. “Simply running and jumping does not improve efficiency.” In addition to more familiar events drawn from human ​sports, robots will ⁠compete in EV charging, restaurant work, emergency incident handling and hand-dexterity contests. There are also industrial assembly and material loading events. A cable connection challenge is a test of vision, mechanical alignment and force control. Beijing-based robotics startup Galbot said it would stage an autonomous humanoid tennis match, ⁠with robots ​attempting singles and doubles play, including ball tracking, serving and returning shots. For Hua ​Rong, chief marketing officer at robotics firm Zeroth, the real test will come after the demonstrations end. “The competition will be whether, after the product is sold, it can ​really solve users’ problems,” she said.

articles.title: France links sharp rise in drownings to prolonged heatwaves
articles.summary: A government minister says people have been taking risks by going into the water, with 301 deaths since 19 June.
articles.body:
France has seen 301 drownings since 19 June, a government minister has said, linking the sharp rise in deaths from last year to a series of prolonged heatwaves.

Sports and Youth Minister Marina Ferrari told France Inter radio the number of deaths - a 14% hike on 2025 - was a "tragic toll".

France, Spain and Italy have all been hit by heatwaves that have triggered massive wildfires that have scorched thousands of hectares of land this summer.

Ferrari said people had been taking risks by going into the water, adding: "Many deadly accidents have occurred in areas that are not authorised or supervised for swimming."

She said a number of the drownings were recorded in "open water, in canals for example".

Ferrari said the government was working with regional authorities "to improve swimming areas and make things safer".

Speaking on Friday, she added that "many drownings, particularly among the elderly, occurred in individual pools".

The minister said that sudden immersion in cold water on a hot day could cause shock, and that in some cases "people can also exceed their physical capabilities".

In June, Ferrari warned that too many people were trying to cool off in rivers and canals without necessarily taking the risks into account.

Climate change is driving up global average temperatures, making heatwaves more frequent and intense.

This has been felt acutely in Europe, which is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service.

Drowning deaths soar in France as Europe buckles in peak of heatwave

A heatwave in June saw a nuclear power plant in south-west France temporarily shut down because water temperatures in the River Garonne topped 28C. Under French laws, water used to cool the reactors at the Golfech plant must not exceed that temperature.

Some monuments like the Eiffel Tower also decided to close early because of the high temperatures in Paris during the heatwave.

The dry conditions also saw wildfires spread across France, with Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux in the south-west of the country, being the worse affected area, with more than 200,000 people being forced from their homes in late July.

France has logged 7,300 excess deaths between late May and 22 July, according to provisional figures from the public health authorities.

articles.title: Iran discovers over 7.5 trillion cubic feet of gas reserves as US blockade squeezes energy sector
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran has discovered more than 7.5 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of natural gas in its southern Fars province, even as months of conflict with the US and I.
articles.body: Iran has discovered more than 7.5 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of natural gas in its southern Fars province, even as months of conflict with the US and Israel have disrupted the country's energy sector.Around 5.7 tcf of the newly discovered gas is recoverable, Iranian oil minister Mohsen Paknejad told state television on Sunday. He said the recoverable reserves were equivalent to around 15 years of production from one phase of South Pars, the world's largest gas field, which Iran shares with Qatar.The discovery also includes gas condensates worth âtens of billions of dollarsâ, Paknejad said, adding that Iran plans to develop the resources âas soon as possible.âHowever, actual production is likely to take years. Iran's energy sector was already struggling with Western sanctions, underinvestment and power shortages before the latest conflict.War hits Iran's gas productionIran lost around a quarter of its daily gas production capacity after attacks on energy infrastructure began in late February, according to Bloomberg. The attacks included strikes on facilities at South Pars.Although some production capacity has since returned, the Iranian government has warned of possible gas shortages this winter and urged citizens to reduce consumption.The latest discovery comes as Tehran faces growing economic and energy pressures amid its confrontation with Washington.Hormuz tensions escalateTensions between the US and Iran also intensified over the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy corridor. US President Donald Trump again shared an image on Truth Social depicting the strategically important waterway as ânew US territoryâ, after sharing the same graphic on August 18. Trump had earlier said, âPretty soon I'll be declaring the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United Statesâ.Iran has rejected the US territorial claims and maintained that the waterway will remain closed unless Washington changes its position.Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei criticised Trump's remarks, saying, âThe gap between America's inability to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and its claim to own it is greater than the 7,000-mile distance between Washington and the Strait itself,â adding, âWelcome to the post-American order in the Persian Gulf.âThe confrontation comes as the US prepares additional economic measures against Tehran. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce what he has described as âthe toughest sanctions in historyâ against Iran and has urged China to cooperate with Washington over Iranian oil shipments.Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei criticised the planned measures, saying, âSuch secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law,â in a post on X on August 22.Rezaei also warned neighbouring countries against supporting the US measures. âWe are telling all nearby countries not to join the US economic war, otherwise we will consider them as enemies,â he said.Despite the escalating rhetoric, Iranian officials have indicated that Tehran remains open to diplomacy. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for diplomatic engagement to resolve the standoff, while stressing that Iran must protect its national strength and dignity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pence: US must prepare for ‘inevitable’ action against Iran
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence argued Sunday the U.S. military should prepare for further strikes against Iran, action he deemed “inevitable.” “It’s going to be absolutely imperative that we keep the pressure on, and that we keep the military assets in the region to be able to take the action that I believe is going…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence argued Sunday the U.S. military should prepare for further strikes against Iran , action he deemed “inevitable.”

“It’s going to be absolutely imperative that we keep the pressure on, and that we keep the military assets in the region to be able to take the action that I believe is going to be inevitable,” Pence told host Dana Bash on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Despite the two sides signing a 60-day memorandum of understanding to pause hostilities in mid-June, the U.S. and Iranian militaries have exchanged strikes since early July.

The violated ceasefire outlined by the memorandum also expired this week , with no public sign of a deal between officials in Washington and Tehran.

President Trump on Wednesday said his administration was ramping up its economic warfare on the Islamic Republic.

In a post on Truth Social , the president wrote that any country that “allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face” economic consequences from the U.S.

Pence on Sunday equated the measures taken by the administration to “D-Day style economic sanctions” — echoing Trump’s rhetoric on Wednesday, when the president argued the sanctions “will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY” for Iran.

But the former vice president also said the Iranians “don’t yet understand that they have been defeated,” citing Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s remarks this weekend on ending the war.

“We are not going to bow our heads,” Pezeshkian said. “We are not going to come humiliated before the enemy. We can stand with power but with logic, and solve our problems.”

Based on that rhetoric, Pence argued the “time’s going to come” for the U.S. and Israel to “finish the job” in Iran.

“You don’t make peace with your enemy,” he told Bash. “You make peace with your defeated enemy.”

articles.title: House Speaker Mike Johnson wants the D.C. IndyCar race to be annual: 'I'll be pushing for that'
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson says he wants the Freedom 250 Grand Prix to return every year. The race was routed to avoid needing congressional approval.
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday he wants to bring the Freedom 250 Grand Prix back to Washington every year.

"I want to bring it back next year. I want to make it an annual event," Johnson told Fox News at the race. Asked whether that was possible, he said: "If we have any say in it, we'll be in the majority. I'll be pushing for that."

The race was designed to avoid Congress. Bud Denker, the Penske Corporation president who built the event, took 81 meetings on Capitol Hill between August and January trying to win approval for a course that ran across Capitol grounds. Federal law bars advertising there, and IndyCars are covered in sponsor logos. Denker was not able to get the votes necessary.

So, Denker moved the circuit a block west, outside congressional jurisdiction, and President Trump signed an executive order on Jan. 30 clearing the way without a vote, CNN reported .

Whether it returns is unsettled. Denker has called this year's race "likely a one-off, in this current iteration, at least." Doug Boles, IndyCar's president, said it is "likely just a one-year event." Mayor Muriel Bowser and Trump have both said they want more races in Washington.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, one of two cabinet officials the order directed to designate the route, told Fox News on Sunday the substitute course turned out better than the original.

"I think this is better. The view of the Capitol behind us," Duffy said. "By the way, this is the first time they're going to sell beer on the Mall of the capital, food, festive car race. So I think this venue is probably better than the original thought anyway."

Johnson said 130,000 people were on the Mall on Sunday and that organizers capped attendance for security. Organizers had said they expected about 140,000 each day, against 288,000 ticket requests.

articles.title: âAttackers took bath, ate datesâ: Chilling details in Bangladesh Hindu family case
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city. Investigators said the suspects allegedly stayed at t.
articles.body: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city. Investigators said the suspects allegedly stayed at the house after the killings, bathed there, ate dates and cucumbers from the refrigerator and used yaba before fleeing, as per local media reports.The victims were identified as retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 23, and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty. Their bodies were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area at around 11.30pm on Saturday.According to Bangladeshâs Prothom Alo, Rangpur police commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud said two suspects, identified as Mugdha and Siddhartha, remained inside the house after the killings. Police said they left on Friday when the streets were relatively empty during Jummah prayers.Before leaving, the suspects allegedly opened cupboards and drawers and scattered clothes and other belongings around the house, apparently in an attempt to make the incident appear to be a robbery. Investigators also found items allegedly used for taking yaba on a table inside the house.Police said evidence was found suggesting that an attempt had been made to test a gold bangle using fire. Two mobile phones belonging to the victims had also allegedly been submerged in water mixed with detergent, possibly in an attempt to destroy evidence.The suspects were identified and detained based on these clues, Prothom Alo reported. Police said they confessed to the killings during questioning. Gold jewellery allegedly looted from the home was later recovered from an abandoned location indicated by the two detainees.Date pits found inside the house have been seized and sent for DNA testing, according to Prothom Alo.The bodies were found in different parts of the house. Subir Chowdhury, in-charge of Rangpur Metropolitan CID, said the mother and daughter were found on the staircase, Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof and Priyamâs body was found under a bed.âThe household belongings were found scattered and in disarray. For now, it appears to be a robbery. However, nothing can be confirmed until the investigation is completed,â he said.Sanatan Chakrabarty, deputy commissioner of Rangpur Metropolitan Police and head of the Detective Branch, said the victims were initially suspected to have been strangled. He said the killings may have taken place between midnight on Thursday and early Friday.The family had not been heard from since Thursday. articles.title: Frustration builds in US city struggling without power for 12 days
articles.summary: In the town of Gary, where a third of residents live in poverty, people say they have been living in "survival mode".
articles.body:
Nearly two weeks after a damaging storm struck her town in Indiana, Terry Dubois is one of tens of thousands of people still without power.

The 77-year-old has been relying on friends to bring her non-perishable food to eat.

Her son brought her a power bank so she can charge her phone and keep in touch with the outside world.

Thankfully, the summer heat hasn't been too punishing, Dubois says, meaning she has not missed her air conditioning too much.

"I've never seen a storm like that in my entire life. Never, never," she tells the BBC.

"It was like a sheer wall of wind," she recalls.

A wave of sudden, severe storms brought flooding and tornadoes to the US Midwest on 11 August, including to Chicago and Indiana, where seven people were killed.

The former industrial town of Gary, which runs along the southern shore of Lake Michigan, was hit particularly hard. Wind gusts peaked at 99mph (159km/h), according to the National Weather Service.

The worst of the storm only lasted five to 10 minutes, but the impacts are lingering 12 days later.

Power has been restored to more than 345,000 customers since the storm struck, but almost 30,000 were still without power as of Sunday morning, according to the area's electrical company Northern Indiana Public Service Company (Nipsco).

In the first few days after the storm, petrol stations, supermarkets and pharmacies were without power, leaving people to survive on what they had.

As the outage stretched into a second week, global food charity World Central Kitchen arrived to help people without access to food.

Power outages are not out of the ordinary for this part of the US. But outages that last more than a week are uncommon.

Once home to the world's largest steel mill, the former industrial heartland of Gary has felt the outage on many fronts. One third of its roughly 70,000 residents live in poverty, according to US Census data.

As well as dealing with storm-damaged properties, residents of the former industrial town have struggled to source food and maintain good hygiene.

There have also been reports of people unable to refrigerate medication and a wheelchair user crawling down their stairs in the absence of working lifts.

At night, some roads have been "pitch black" without working street lights, Gary resident Kyle Allen tells the BBC.

Allen has faced shorter power outages before, but this experience has been different as he has started caring for his 95-year-old father.

As a result, he bought a generator which has been sustaining him and his father since the power failed.

Shatiya Hardin, meanwhile, said the situation has been "absolutely horrible".

"At night we're sweating, we're irritable, we have children to look out for, elderly people who need electricity for oxygen tanks," she told the BBC's US partner CBS.

"It's not OK for us to continually be in survival mode."

Amid mounting frustration, local residents have launched a class-action lawsuit, accusing the utility company Nipsco of failing to manage the trees that brought down the power lines in the storm.

In the lawsuit, resident Jack Tipold said he was in the middle of dental surgery when the power failed.

He said he was forced to abandon the procedure and was discharged without adequate pain medication.

"I had all my teeth removed and no medication for 48 hours. Let me tell you something, it was a struggle," he told CBS.

Nipsco has denied wrongdoing and said it would "vigorously" defend itself in court.

Faith leaders alarmed by the ongoing outage held a news conference on Saturday outside a local church.

"We come together today with one voice, asking those who have the power... to release the resources to our brothers and our sisters, our mothers and our fathers, because 12 days is long enough," he said, according to the Indianapolis Star.

Nipsco said on Sunday that it was restoring power to everyone as soon as possible and estimated Gary would have its electricity restored by Wednesday.

"We recognise how frustrating and difficult it is to be without power for an extended period," the company said in a statement.

Indiana's Governor Mike Braun said on Sunday that there was "no excuse for these delays".

He has requested a quicker major disaster declaration from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema), which would unlock further help.

With climate change making extreme weather more severe and frequent, such power outages are likely to become a more common problem.

In the meantime, Braun has pushed Nipsco to bring in more crews to get those without power back online, telling the firm: "Put every available resource into the field. Get creative."
